blocks.x: The first thing I'd like to ask you is your name.
Cassius Wilson. Cassius Wilson. Cassius, yes. C-A-S-S-R-U-S. C-A-S-S-R-U-S.
C-A-S-S-R-U-S. Cassius Wilson.
C-A-S-S-R-U-S.
Cassius Wilson. And, uh, let's see, this is the first reel we're doing on here. And what's today's date?
I don't know speaking for Reed.
They're like that. Let me put this on here. This is Real 2, Cassius Wilson, April 5, 1962. You were saying people had a better time in the old days.

Oh, yeah. No, they had a better time in all of these. There's more places to go now than it was then. Because when I was a young man, you had to be 21 years old to go in the ballroom. You couldn't go there and fool the man, the owner, the place, the bartender, you tell him you're 21. You couldn't lie in them. Not anything goes in the ballroom. Well, they come along and say, how old are you? I'm 18 or 19. Go ahead. But we couldn't get by with that kind of stuff. No, we couldn't get by with that. I was 18 years old. I couldn't look in the ballroom. But today, there's so many places. Like my little brother, he's just 17 years old. Go to all them places. I couldn't go in them. The young people is more free now than they was in the olden days. Now they had a hall around here. We call it a corporate hall. And the economy hall. Now if a young girl would go to a dance, she went with some of her parents. It had to be her brother, her uncle, her mother, her sister, her aunt. And that certain amount of hours was, say, 11 o'clock, 11.30, they had to leave. They left. They went home. Then the sporting class of people would come on. They'd come on. They'd always break up at two o'clock in the morning, sometimes four in the morning. Well, they just mixed like they do now. Everybody's together now. But in those times in certain classes, you bump by yourself, I bump by myself. And we had a bunch of men on that corner over there. When a younger man bumped on his corner, he didn't bump the older man. Didn't drink with him. He wasn't asking for a match. We didn't allow it. But I was a young fella. And I went out in that Orange Channel. And I was a man before guys even knew I drank. They tried all kinds of ways. And I used to gamble. We'd catch that slack poker. And they'd allow me to gamble with them. And they'd buy a dress and offer a drink, but I never drink. And I used to put these within a, I ain't gonna make that fella drunk. He didn't know myself, you ain't gonna make this fella drunk. A long time before I started drinking. And now I don't drink much now. I'll drink a few beers. I never go out through the week unless it's something important, a meeting, something like that. When I come from down there around this time of the, I was digging here, I sat out there while I got television in the back. I went in here, I got a radio back there. That dogma thing, I don't know when I played that thing, that music box.
But you said there were plenty of places in the old days, huh, where you could go to the end of the day.

Well yeah, that's why I mean like the lake, Spanish food, West End, all those places where you could go and that's why most of the people would go. Now, Millenburg was a great big place, you go bathing and it had camps all along. They had a band that played out there, you see, in them different camps. Well, we'd go in from one camp to another, one camp to another, one camp to another. They'd charge me for forty cents or fifty cents to go in and dance. You could rent a bathing suit if you wanted or brought your own bathing suit and go bathing. Well, it's nothing like that. The only place they got now is way out here in the woods, little woods. And it's so obvious getting out there. But a lot of people's out there, though. Christ, woods, people go out there. Well, I never grew up there. You know, I don't like the crowd no more. I don't care for the crowd. No, I don't care for the crowd.
But you liked Millenburg and West End and Spanish food when you were younger?

Well, in those days we even had the fairground. They would give, like these big bands would come out of the city, come here to the city, well they'd go and play at the fairgrounds, the Oddfellas, and the Knights of Piffion, and all those fellas, they'd give things. Each year those people used to parade at big parades. The Oddfellas, then the Knights of Piffion, then the Mason, well all those fellas used to parade. They don't parade no more, nothing but they also parade. But those times all those societies, and the young men, Olympians, and all them people, they were societies, but they'd parade every year. It's just a fair. We the only, the Elks, and well you might catch the scabber clubs, come around. But those clubs, they would parade yearly. Just like we do now, the Jolly Boys. Now we the only club that really parades yearly. They had the Bulls. They had the Tanami. Well all those fellas used to parade. The Hobgobblers. That's in the olden times. Every week it was a parade. But now they did. The younger fellas, he don't want to spend no money, and the older fellas had died out. So my club, they like that parade, and we got a lot of young fellas. So I'll tell you how they do now. See like this time of year, we'll all have a hundred and a hundred and fifty members. See? They want to parade. And you cannot parade unless you join the club. You got to be a member of the club to parade. So we have them coming in now like nobody's business. But after the parade, out they go. And they'll come back the next year, and then put in that membership. Stay in it maybe two months, three months. Then after that, they're going to get a dropout. We keep around forty-five, fifty, seventy-five, standing number. But they're in year in, year out. A lot of those old fellas, they don't parade, but they just stay in the club. Because they like the club. And we have a banquet, and then we have, we used to give an annual picnic, because it cost us about five hundred dollars. But it didn't cost the members nothing. The club just put that on for all the people and their families. We used to go down there to do foes. Well, the place got some beds and there's some nasty out there. Every time it'd go out there, it'd rain, and the yard wasn't sufficient. Well, this year I'm going to try to take them over the lake. Yeah, we'll try to get them over the lake this year.
Do you hire a band when you have a picnic?

Yes, oh yeah. The band would play all day. Well, see we'd buy ten barrels of beer, see ten barrels of beer. We'd bring them barrels of beer. When we give all the way. All the people bring us their lunch, bring their baskets, and we furnish all the soft drinks and all the beer you want to drink, and transportation. That's what it costs so much. And then we have to pay for a band. Yeah, we'd get three buses. And a lot of people, when I sat down there, they couldn't get their bus. City public service bus, a lot of them going automobile. A lot of people don't want to go until in the afternoon. And a lot of people, a lot of them, people, they'd cheer on them. But their youngsters could have somebody.
What bands would you hire?

Well, any of them that we can get. We don't make no difference. We can get any of them. We get, let's call it H. Yes. Well, we mostly, well, see H's daddy was the president of the club at one time. Fred Minor. Well, then Fred resigned as president of the club. But he still was, we carried him as a passage member until he died. Well, then, to Fred we used to get eight.
That's Fred's son.

But he gave us good music. Well, yeah, he gave us good music. He gave us all that we wanted. So we hired John, we hired John Kazma. Any good band we know. We know it's a good band. Just like when we give a dance. We always try to get the good music. You see when you've got a good band you pour the crowd. If you don't have a good band you don't pour no crowd. Just like in my time we used to, there was a hall on Liberty Street, you see, called it, that was the cooperators. And they had one right here on the whistle on the street. That was the cooperators and the economy. The economy. Well now, the point is you wonder who's playing at the economies? Sam Morgan. Who's playing at the other one? Rainey. Well you like Rainey, I like Sam. Well I'm going by the cooperators because Sam was playing there. Well he played beautiful music. Soft. And Rainey played loud music, you know. Now he went down, the Rainey. He had a good band. Well drinking that caused him Rainey going down, Rainey drinks over. I heard him at the end.
Huh? Yeah, well he was shocked.
That's what happened with a lot of them fellows. They just drink, drink. I don't know. Punch is strong now. He's coming back, Punch. Yeah, yeah, yeah.
I'm telling you he's coming back. I'm glad to see him well because I thought he was going to leave us for a while.
I did too. I'm glad to see him well because I thought he was going to leave us for a while.

I did too. I'm glad to see him well because I thought he was going to leave us for a while. My doctor thought he had cancer but he didn't. It turned out it was his gallbladder, gallbladder. But it looked like cancer for a while. Mm-hm. Why those guys don't take care of themselves, you see? They play music like I didn't know they bum all night.
They really play music like I didn't know they bum all night. They really play music like I didn't know they bum all night. They really get through playing and then they go to drinking and bumming.
I notice most of the old ones take pretty good care of themselves now.

I'm glad they do. I was talking to him. He's in the record band and he told me. He said, I got enough of it already. I got enough of it already. He said, I can't think too much of it. He said, I can't think too much of it. He said, I tell them that too. See, I got them for five or six hours. After that I didn't want no more of it. Well I'll tell you, I was talking to John and John was telling me, he said, you willing to play for them, he says, how many hours? I said, I can't make eight hours. He said, I'll play for them. He said, you know, and we don't have to have a nickel for John to play. John, he won't take no deposit. Just tell him we want to send his dime. He's throwing the ball. But he had to get eight hours no more. I tell you, John is about sixty-some years old.
Who can be a member of your club, by the way? Who can join your club?
Well, we just, I mean, I got a good character and he's all right. I'm not a bad fella. There's always somebody vouch for him, you know.
But you have to pass on him somehow, I mean, a membership.

Well, yes, yes they do. They have to pass the decision. If they don't know him, they investigate him. And if they know him, a lot of fellas that we have in our club, the most of them is right around our neighborhood. We know them all. And they in and out. We don't have them. Only time we get strange fellas is like, like this time of year when we're gonna parade. We get fellas from Weaver Industries Canal, anywhere, called them. We know they in there that's what we're gonna parade. Yeah. Yeah, we know that.
Well, how do they pay their dues?

Well, they come up on Sunday. Every month? Every month, yeah, once a month. You see we have two meetings a month. We have the first and the fourth Sunday. And the two later have the second and the fourth Sunday.
You can't make them all. It looks like all those clubs, if they all meet at the same time.

Well, you don't have to go to meet. If you go to meet this Sunday, well you don't have to go, if you make the two land the first Sunday, you don't have to make them no more until the next month. But you make the Jolly Boys the last Sunday. Well most of the fellas that sends their money in, they don't come to meet. They send it in there. Now my secretary has a list stacked that high with the people's name. It'd be right around the corner. And if they won't come to meet, they give me the dollar. They send me a dollar and ten cents a month. They send that dollar and ten cents. And then if I know a fella and he wants to join the club, I mean he's in the club and he's all right, well I'll pay for him. So and so and so. Well we don't, well you see you can't be with two months in the rear. Well all you want, the next month out you go unless somebody pay for you. Well I pay a lot of them fellas that don't get my money back though. Now my wife have a cousin around there, he belongs to Jolly Boy. He don't want a club but he owe me. He don't want a club nothing. He come there, come here a couple of Sundays ago. He says he paid his tax and he paid his due. But he owe me a treat all of them dude. He said he didn't pay me. He said well I'm going to straighten you out. I said okay, all right, go. Pay me as well you know. Pay me as well. Now we got a little fella wait for the checker cab company. See we have a dance, each member is tight for two tickets. Well this little fella got two tickets and he didn't pay and he got out. Now he wants to come back. Now he sent his fees but he didn't send him tickets, that ticket money they turned him down. So I kept his fees there for a whole month. Two months. Eventually he sent the dollar and a half, paid for his two tickets. They took him back in the club. But he's just in there for the parade. After the parade he can get out again.
How old does a man have to be to join the Jolly Boy? 18 to 65. 18 to 65. Once you hit 65 you can't join? No, after you get over that. Well we got some of them in there over that.

But that's the rule. We have a lot of youngsters. Around 8, 7, 15, 16 years old, 13 years old, they parade with us. We don't charge them nothing to parade. All they do is just buy their parents, buy their clothes and they... We'll have maybe eight to ten youngsters, brothers like that. All up. They don't charge them nothing to parade. Because you can't join the club, they do young, but we just let them come out. Now this fellow Madelea, he asked me Sunday about the... It's his boy. I think his boy was out with us Sunday, he was. When he's tall, he's a little, but he's young. He said, what we gonna do about his boy? I said, buy his clothes and they don't even come out. That's all. I'm gonna have to take it away. What's the purpose of the Jolly Bunch? Well, what you say, Jolly Boys. Just a lot of lively fellas. That's what a name, Gumpo. They like sport. They like to eat and drink. And of course, we'll name this the Jolly Bunch. But when they get together, they all like to drink and eat. So as they meetin', after meetin', they'll have sandwiches and beer and whatever they wanna drink. How much money they got? If they got fifteen dollars, they drink up to fifteen dollars. You see? But now it's just a little different. Now because we don't take care of the sick. We're not an aide. We're a pleasure. We don't aid. Now, two lands are an aide. But the Jolly one's not an aide. It's just strictly a pleasure. We used to give four enterprises a year. We spent seventy-five, eighty, ninety dollars every three months, eat and drink. Well, that's what the most of the people's in there for. You wanna tell the truth, you know, drinking. They don't have to buy it. That's all. That comes out of the treasure. But we have a debt fund. We have to give those people what we promised them. And we have two bank accounts. One for pleasure, one for death. You can't use that death fund unless somebody dies. But that pleasure, you can do what you want. Well, if you break it, it's all right. So now they're trying to build their pleasure fund back up. And last, the young people last, they had a picnic. That picnic cost us $5,500. And not without taxing the members. And these things can't be done without tax. You just can't do it on this dude. And thirty-five percent of your dues go to the debt fund. One of these guys right there at the table, every time a dollar goes across, a dollar and ten cents go across there, he gets thirty-five cents out of that. Well that don't be taxed at all. We got two treasures. One strictly for the debt fund, and one for the pleasure. Because if we didn't do that, some guy would jump up and make a move that we should have so and give so and so and so. When I have to take all of my debt fund, now we're going to lose a member. Now we're trying to get away from that tax, you see, for membership. A member died when we were trying to get away from that tax. If we can build up enough in our debt fund, we won't have to do that. So we're going to refine it. No.
Your tax a club when a member dies, in other words?

Yeah, one dollar. In fact, all these clubs and societies do that. All of them. I've lost a couple of women's society in there. Because they don't end as hard on it as a man, because they only charge sixty-five cents and seventy-five cents. Now right now I've got two men in the two lands to pay for, that's two dollars. I've got two sons and daughters I know, well that's sixty-five cents each. I don't know how many more, well that's only most of the old people, you see. I don't know how many more, but I know that's the last I heard. Of course I won't owe any money until May. I paid up from January to June. Well I didn't know anything. So the girl said, well you got two members here. I know this brother, the last two members died, that belongs to those women's society. And also the two ladies. And one of those guys I come near paid for him in the Jolly Boys, but he got out the Jolly Boys. So we got out just in time. But I'd have to pay for him.
What's the sons and daughters, which one is that?
It's a, it's a, it's like a benevolent. It's like a benevolent.
What's the full name of it? Just the sons and daughters? Sons and daughters.
Sons and daughters. Sons and daughters. Is it called benevolent association? They have the sons and daughters.
They have the lady tannemys. They have the lady two names.

They have the lady two names. They have the lady one hundreds. We're all in the meeting at the two-lane club. They're all in the meeting at the two-lane club. They're all in the meeting at the two-lane club.
And how do you, how does it work if you should be in a ladies society? Can you be an officer there?

Well, no, they have men and ladies in it too. You see, they have ladies and men and men. See, but our club, the two-lane have all the men and the men two-lane. And we have a lady jolly bunch. Yeah, we have a lady jolly bunch. But we have nothing to do with their business. They have nothing to do with our business. But a ladies club, all the officers are women or can some of them be men? Oh, yes, yes, yes, both men. A lady two-lane got men.
Men officers?

Yeah, they got men. The president's a man. Yeah, he's a man. But most of them women clubs, they got women presidents. Yeah, most of them. It's called Maxson. His name is Maxson. Well, he's a president of the lady two-lane. But all the rest of those women's society have women.
Do you sing at meetings, by the way?
Hmm?
Do you sing at meetings?
No, we just open with a prayer and close with a prayer.
I know some of the clubs do.

Yes, some of them do. Yes, some of them do. Most of them ladies do. There's two-lane dozen. And he was the jolly boy for a lot of those men. Now we have a club down here that are Wonder Bowl-wise. Omero, 1600 Bowl? Well, you know all them jolly boy. Well, you know all them jolly boy. I went to a wedding reception. Yeah, well they got a nice place. Mice belongs to that. Yeah, mice belong to it. Mice is, there's something in there, I don't know what mice is, there's something in the Wonder Boy. But I don't like the Wonder Boy for one particular reason. There's no benefit, no kind of way for you in the Wonder Boy. There's this two and a half you just put in there, just throwing it away. And I can't see no sense in that, you don't get no plus out of it or nothing. I had an application and I went down and looked at the place and they got to play pool, you know, they got to pool hall upstairs and bar upstairs. But I couldn't see why putting two dollars and a half in a club with nothing behind it, it don't give you no benefit at all. Not even if they give you a barrel, a band of music, you know, something for your money, but they don't give me nothing. What do they do with the money? Building funds, buying a building. They all go live long up with all the buildings. The two land, they have a banquet, different layouts, and of course we are the best, the Jolly Pudge. We're the best. We do more, have more pleasure than any of them clubs. Spends more money than them spend.
In olden times, did they spend much money on their clothes when they had the thick hair?

Well, the... Marais, I mean? No, they mostly, in olden times, when they turned out, they had black suits. They didn't turn out like these fellas turn out the day, but they all decorate umbrellas. You know how it cost them 15, 12 dollars to decorate one of them umbrellas? I'm telling you. Fans, they decorate their fans in the umbrellas. They have a fan umbrella and a basket. That's right. I want to see how they carry it all. Well, it's sad. They'll be having it. They don't need all that. I wouldn't want an umbrella in a basket, me, myself. But they'll have it. You'll see them if you live long enough. You'll see them in an umbrella and a basket. I was talking about how much it's going to cost them to every is umbrella made. But I never didn't have a basket. I only had a fan. Because I've been an officer for years, too. I was just riding an automobile. Yeah, I'd ride an automobile and get tired and we'd just cut out. If we got to stop, say, 10 blocks away, well, we'll just go there and get out the automobile and get a couple of beers and wait until they get there. And every one fault I find I would raise a second line. We just get them guys off the street. They're all right, but I don't know, you just can't get them out the street. The police can't do nothing with them.
It cost you a thousand dollars to hire enough policemen to take them away.

That's right. That's really a fact. You never have many police, you've got to have your help in the parade. When they get in that procession, and as you go along, you're picking them up. About a 20, 150 cent. They got a gang down there that's the umbrella game. They comes out with their own umbrellas. Well, I've seen that crowd and they can really be kind of rough. They is rough. They too rough. And that's the street not on food with them because they too rough. They don't worry me because I don't parade. And I hasn't been parading. They asked me, Mice asked me, was I coming out? I said, no indeed. Mice thinks this is the fifth year I am parading. It's the sixth year. I said, I don't know what to do. What are you going to do? They put them in jail and all that. That's what's to use. It's just a rough gang. And I was in hope they would never parade no more myself. I said, I have to go up there. I'll be up there and see them all. And to see if they get everything arranged right and that. I'll go back. We had a dance at night, you know. And I'll go back and be at the dance. Mice is chairman of the dance. He's going to parade. Mice is chairman of the dance. He's assistant chairman of the parade. I don't see how he can make it all that. Well, I'll tell you how they wake that out. He's an officer. He rides mostly at the time. And around about 4 o'clock, 4.30, when he'll cut out, go home and think. He wants to come back until about 9, 10 o'clock. He's got an assistant who was really everything arranged before the parade. And his assistant won't parade. You see, he'll be right on the job. We have a standard committee, yearly committee. And they take care of everything. So we just appointed chairman for the Sunshine of the Enterprise. And those fellas take over. Is that the name, Bella? Yeah, they take over. Ice up, beer up, then put behind the ball. They're very dutiful. They like to help their club out. Yeah.
Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Every year. Every year president.

Every year. Every year. Every year. and we have our relation of officer in March and we installed them in April. We're Sunday in March is our relation of officer and we have installed in May. Of course, I've been vice president for about 10 years. Yeah, well, I could have taken over a long time, but I just didn't want the responsibility. But the fellow with the last fellow, our president, he just did so wrong and we had to do it with him. His name was David Glenn. So I've been active for nearly a whole year. Of course, they wants me. They likes me. Everybody likes me. Everybody likes me. Everybody likes me.
You say you have a president, a vice president? Yeah. And you have any kind of secretary? I recall the secretary, the final secretary,

and she had one of the finance. She had one of the first dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear
This is the fan.
This is the fan. No, they don't be all made like this. That's decorated. All of them have fans similar to that, but different style of fans, but they have different decorations.
Who decorates the fan?
Well, we have certain people can decorate them. Now this is a badge. You have to have this badge. The vice president.
It's got long ribbons and a flower on it.

Just like that, you see, all of them will be that way. And the members will have the same badge, but on that white it will be membership. The president will have his president. Then the secretary, the treasurer, whatever position it is, it's on his badge.
Does the club have any special colors or just those of the club colors? Yellow and is that blue or blue?
Well, it's white. It's supposed to be bluish, but blue. Then I get them days away.
And you have those same colors every year on your badge?

Oh yeah, the badges be made the same every year. One particular man makes the badges. Anybody can decorate a fan, they'll decorate the fan for you. Well, they got a lot of girls decorate your fans. Now this fan is about five years old.
That's about the fanciest fan I think I've ever seen.
Oh yeah, you know, you can't buy them. They don't have you to tell them of me.
Yeah, I do.

Oh yeah, they make these fans. They don't make the fan, they take the fan. They buy an ordinary fan out of there like the, maybe McCoy or some of those places. And some of them have the big round ones, you know, different design of what they want. And then they decorate them. But how they decorate them, I don't know.
Well that one's covered with ribbon and that. That's right.
That's right. Jim's wife did that.
Which Jim?
The little place up there. What was that? The little bar?
Oh, Jim's place.
Yeah, his wife did that. Josephine. Now she decorate the basket and fan. Then part of the chicken maker. So I just keep this one still vanilla. That's all.
Just got a, looks like a flower made out of those ribbons on it.

Uh huh. Well this is the shape of the fan's in. And it was not in the shape this way. Well all they do is, oh it's beautiful one that's, I mean, for it's made because all that'd be puffed out, you see. Because it's been packed in, things are packed on top of it. I don't think there's nobody in the parade that had a fan like this. The only one had this style of fan.
Everyone's fan is different then?

All of them is different. Different designs, different colors. Just like their baskets. The baskets are decorated, different they have a basket. Oh I guess it sets about that high. About three feet almost. Oh yes, some of them are so tall that guy, when he's walking he's got to hold this away. He can't hold it down. He's got to hold it up. Now mostly your marshal pretty much has the extra large basket. Your marshal of the day, I think he's the first man, that's the grand marshal. He's leading the whole procession. Well he has a great big bag, big basket and a great big fan and he's going on patting and kicking the whole thing. I just want to leave. He used to be practically a regular grand marshal. Nobody didn't run against him and they wanted him, he's tall you know. And that's the kind of man you need for a grand marshal, a tall man. Like that big fella was out there Sunday, those are the kind of fellas for grand marshal. Well we have two big fellas for the parades of marshal, Willie Hicks and his fella named Cass, they call him. He's a great big fella too. Why would you need a big fella? Well he's tall and you can see him coming. You can see him coming. That second line can't hide him.
He looks good out there. Oh he looks better good.

Yeah. And he got a dove up here or something on his shoulder and he got that sash across here. And the grand marshal has a great big sash and he got to hold it up. He's got it on his arm. Oh they wouldn't take nothing for that day.
Well how come you had those two marshals in front, those two fellas in front this Sunday?
Well we, those are our two regular marshals.
No no I mean Fats Houston and Slowdrag, the big guy.

Oh I don't know that they, they brought those fellas there you see. But now that's what, that's what all the hump was. That was all the kick about. The club didn't want to march behind them. They didn't want to do the, put their own grand marshal there but this little fella there?
The fella that signed the contract? Yeah. Jaffe, you're on Jaffe.

Well he wanted this fella see. But see we should, see my marshal should have led the band, then my second marshal should have led the club. So that's the way we turned out. I have a number one marshal, he leads the procession. And my second grand marshal, he leads the members, the banner. But as he wanted like that, well we let him go head on like that. But we don't, we have, if we're gonna turn out, they didn't like the colors. They didn't like the colors. I told them what don't make any difference, well that we all, otherwise we're just filling in to help them fellas out and we're doing the job. We're not parading, we're not paying for nothing. See if we had to pay for that band then nobody else would never got that, no indeed. I told them what we ain't paying for nothing, we don't care. They paid you in other words. I told them they're paying us so let them have it. Of course I know slow drags all for years. Slow drags an old, old time. And in fact all them guys, it was poke chops and that gang, I know all them fellas. Poke chops used to be a member of my old club, he prayed with us once or twice. He was out of the parade, he don't stay on stage, he's gone. Now we have a fellow around Jim's, he's called him Rankin. He can run poke chop in dancing. And you think that guy will get out there and dance? Now he'll get rid of them barrooms and cut up and dance. Poke chop ain't got a chance with him. What do you eat now? Poke chop had him out in the French bars once or twice. And he don't like that. He just like to, like we all, he likes to drink. And we'll all be sitting here drinking, and he'll get up on the floor and dance himself down. Hey, I wish I had this talent, I wish I could dance like that, I'm telling you. And let's just throw it away. And then start, he was dancing Sunday with me. You know what I mean? He danced Sunday with me.
Yo, I saw one guy doing that, I'm going to get out and everything.
Oh yeah, they got a lot of pictures of that guy too. They took a lot of pictures of that fellow.
Well he looked like an alligator the way he walked on.
Yeah, he sure did.
Hey Alan, that walker's the way.
And he always, I don't care when we have a funeral. I don't know where he comes from, but he's out there with him.
That's what I wondered sometimes when I've been to some funerals down here. How does everybody find out about him? I don't know.
I don't know why they found it, but they find it.
The band tells me, but I know everybody.

Well, that's what happened. The people of the day, I don't care, right now, you let a band pass out, right out there, we don't know nothing's going on. And you'll see people coming from all directions. The last time they had a funeral from down here, this boy, he played with, you mean Papoose? Yeah, he played with Fat Dominic. He died in California. Or New York, I think it was. He died in New York. Well his daddy, called Walter, he played the guitar out there as well. Now Slowdrag, him, Noon, well they used to go around and play together. But mostly Walter, Sam, and Noon. Noon made his own, Noon made his own, and they used to go around and serenade in different places, all around the French Quarter. But I don't know, those fellas like they get, they're trifling. Now Walter, his son played music, his wife played music, his daughters, his sisters play music, all them play guitar. He played music, and he played music. That little boy was a wonderful thing. He got in that dope racket, that's what happened to him. That overdose, that killed him. Well when they buried him, the Caledonia, well the Caledonia, the front of the Caledonia furnished the music. They didn't have nobody out but the second line in the band. So I said to the fellas, I said, well why is it members? It ain't no Caledonia, which I know it's no Caledonia. I said, ain't no members. I said, look at the members out there with the umbrella. And they goes down there, and the next block, on the next Long Street, where Delio used to be, I forgot to call the girls' name, Ogapiku, that's what joint. And them people stayed in there about four hours. And our men, you wouldn't have walked, it wasn't carnival they, down that block. They went in that place, the band went inside and they stayed in there. And they were like, well a lot of the time we have a funeral and then we wind up back at the Tulane Club, we go back in the hall and join them. They played four or five members for them. And my wife now loaded down. Yeah, it goes.
Did you ever hire a rock and roll band to play for your dancers? Yes. You have rock and roll?

Yeah, we had this boy, Dookie Chase, young Dookie Chase, he played for us. And this band I'm telling you about, no, I can't call a name of them youngsters, they're a rock and roll band, they play good music too.
And the members like that?

Oh yes, we had them twice, we had our 42nd dance, we gave this year we had that same band. And that, yeah. Those guys can sing, you know, they got plenty of people. And that's what the young people want today. They want that, that, that rock and roll stuff.
Well what about, as a rule, would you hire a band say like John Casimir's or H's or a rock and roll band? Which of the members prefer?

Well sometimes they can't get those rock and roll bands, sometimes they'd be hired at that particular date. So in that time you have to get the band to have an opening date. Well John plays good music, he plays good enough music for everybody, they like it really. They have so many bands now, I'll tell you the truth, I can't even keep up with them, that play for these dancers. Yeah. So many of them. But this last band we had, they were very young, around 17, 18, 19 years old. But they play music. Yeah they play music. But mostly all that rock and roll stuff. And that's what the youngsters want today. And they just takes the flow. Oh yeah they takes the flow.
What about the olden time brass bands? Could you tell me a little bit more about that? Who's that? Some of the olden time brass bands.

Well we had, Celestan, he was an old brass band. Well Louis played too. Louis was a, he played parades and fumes in his time. We had Joe Oliver, he played for these dances, he played for fumes and parades. Well in Dallas time they used to play for the Carnival Parades. They had to play for Carnival Parades. No school band didn't play for Carnival Parades like they do today. That's why they had so many bands, because those colored bands used to play for all that. That was their job in my time. They played for all these parades.
What neighborhood did you say you were brought up in?
I was brought up in the Irish Channel. That's around Diamond and South Peter. Enunciation Street, Chappatula Street, St. Thomas Street.
Did they have many Carnival clubs up there when you were young?
No they didn't. We had one club up there. They were all in the back of town. Zulus, Canemys, Bulls, all those clubs were back here. Hop Goblins were all in the back of town.
What was the one up in Channel?

Well we had, we just had the, oh no, what the name was like that club. We paraded at that time, in that time, and then they, well that was around 17, 18, 19, 18, 1917, just before the war. Then during the war they broke up. Of course I left, when I went to the Army in 17, and when I come out the Army, I left for my neighborhood altogether. And I've been down here and down there ever since I've been down here for 50 years.
Did it seem very different down here? The music was the same band?

Well, that's in the olden time. You know how first, see? They don't do the things. They didn't have much sport. We used to always have to come back for such things as dances and things. We all had to come back at that time. We all had to come back at that time for everything. It was nothing out there but a lot of work, warehouses, big drays, different drays out there. And people scattered about. In my days there was a lot of gambling. There was a lot of gambling. In other words you could, they'd give you a charter to gamble. There was a lot of gambling clubs out there. Most people would go out there because they had plenty of money. See? But there were back down here where they had all the, but I don't know what you all call them. Places where they had the piano, the drum, and the horn. Well, that was all across Ramport Street. You had to get the Ramport Street to catch all that. You mean the tongue. That's right. And that was all back this way. And out of my way, well, we had one or two of them scattered about there. We had one at Diamond and South Peter. Well, we had a piano and one show back on Saturday and Sunday. You know, but most of the idiots out there was gambling. We've been gambling, that's all.
Well, who were the piano players? Do you remember any of them?

Well, yes. I remember a wood of them. We had some wonderful piano players. That's some of these, well, in these late years, right around here, youngsters. This boy Burnell, he's one of the best. And that boy could wake his finger like an electric piano. The dope killed him. We got another man called Little Willie. The dope killed him. See, one of the things about them, and see, if they were using the right stuff, but they would get that junk. And that junk just knocks them out. Where's Red Caillou, he was a wonderful little piano player, and they used to buck. They used to buck. They'd come in the place, five or six of them, and one off the stool, the other's on, one off the stool, the other's on, just bucking against one another. And boy, you'd be talking to something. Well we should have, we should have appetized for a dance. The bands would meet on the corner sometimes, three bands. Just stay out there an hour. Chris Kelly, Rainey, and a punch. Or Sam Morgan, Chris Kelly, and Rainey. They'd always meet, and we'll see at those times we'd have appetized for a dance. Like we were going to give a dance at the economy hall, at the car operators hall, or the France Army. They'd get a, there wasn't no trucks at that time. Yes it was trucks, that's right. They'd take a truck, put a big sign on it, and the band would be in the truck. And they'd stop at each corner and play while they got a ballroom. And they'd sometimes all meet, sometimes four bands would be on one corner. And they'd steady hours at this plane, one after another. That's why I said they don't have a time now that we hadn't, we'd come along. Because the band would, now my club was giving a dance, we'd have a time for that dance. Well yeah we'd have a time for that dance. Hire that band, hire that truck. And they'd go all around, we wouldn't go too far out of our neighborhood, you know, way uptown. We'd go around where we know it's going to bring the people that are going to come. And somebody else had got a dance, they hire a truck. And they'd all meet and they'd play out there for hours at a time. There was plenty of pleasure then. There wasn't fights like we did today, you know, killing like you do now. We just drink and have fun.
Back to these piano players, do you remember Gang Kid?
Who?
Gang Kid. He played around up there, up front. I don't know what I know him. Drive them down.

Yes I know him. Drive them down. Drive them down. And we had a fellow, he used to play around parties, and the deals around that. We used to call him, his name was Thomas. In other words he was a ballast music player, we had ballast music, but that's what the people wanted in my day. Oh yeah. They wanted those blues and you know.
Thomas played piano or some of the-
Oh yeah, he was a good piano player, you know, he was a good piano player.
Have you had many guitar players in places like that?
Well I don't know too many guitar players.
Like Rabbit I'm thinking about.

Well I know all them fellas, Rabbit and this boy Walter down there, he'd run that place down there, I'm telling you not. He's a bartender there now. Now I don't know if Noon stopped playing, is he playing yet? Yeah he's playing. He's playing yet? He plays yet? Huh? But no, there was a kick, so them guys used to come around and from one place to another him and Sam and his boy was like, I don't know if he was playing. He's playing. He's playing. He's playing. He's playing. He's playing yet? He plays yet? Yeah, well I saw him Sunday and I saw him Sunday and I saw him Sunday. But no, there was a kick, so them guys used to come around and from one place to another to him and Sam and his boy Walter. You know, and you hear that music? Just stop in front of your door and just play that music. And this boy Sam could sing. Yeah he could sing. And they'd come in here and stay in here for the day, just play and sing. I don't see much of those fellas. I don't know where I knew him to be at.
Serenading has dropped off. Well they all bum at Buster's you know. Oh yeah. At Orleans and Burgundy.
Oh yeah. That's why I see no one most of the time doing on Burgundy Street. When I'm passing the bus because I'm looking out. I see no one. Drag. Nah this boy Sam I don't know where he's at.
I haven't seen him in a while.
No I haven't seen him in a long time. He's a little back at the man near Galvis. I don't know what to come of Sam.
He and them were real tight one for that. Oh was he?
Oh boy. Them guys was alright. Something happened he doesn't work with them anymore. No. We don't get together no more.
When did you hear drive him down to play piano? Oh Lord when's I heard him? When's I heard a piano player you mean?
My wife's nephew is a wonderful piano player and do you know I never heard him play?
Never had heard him play? No. No.

But I mean did you hear him someplace like the Spanos or the Red Onion or something? Well those are the kind of places I used to hear all those piano players. But after those places without existing you know right over here at one time they had a
piano. That corner.

The bottom of the day I think it took the piano away from the people, the damn music boxes. That ruined it. Because every place had a piano in it. And somebody was there, but that higher man especially, they were like, you know, the high man's spotter at weekends just to play piano. But now the music box took that away from them. Put your nickel in there now. Get your music. What you gonna do?
Well do people have more or less time for that kind of thing now than they used to?

Well, I don't know what they call, they have better time, and we have what they think, that's what they call. Well they're more freer. They got more joints to go in. And they do more than we did. See? And we respect the public. In my time we respect the public. People don't respect nobody. Not this young generation coming up today. They don't respect nobody. But we did. We wouldn't say a bower in front of a lady of no kind. We respect all of them. White or black, but the people today don't respect nobody. I'll tell you what I think about it though. I think the people of the day drink some more wine than I did when I come along. You very seldom, if a man would drink wine, he'd go in and say, give me a glass of wine. Would they give you a little glass of wine like that? That was it. But today they get a jug of wine. And two people walk up down the street with that jug of wine on their shoulder. But in my days, we had more respect for ourselves than the youngsters got today. See, I can't put us walk up down the street with bottles of beer and bottles of wine. We didn't do nothing like that.
But did they smoke hop in those times? Well, yes.

But you see, a man smoke hop, he stayed to himself. A man used dope, he stayed to himself. He didn't bum all together like they do today. If you was a dope addict, you had your bunch. And like I knew, when you used dope, well why didn't it associate with you at all? But now they're all together, you don't know who's who. I remember when you could get a moot of cigarette, two for fifteen. That's right. Two for fifteen?
Two for fifteen.

Two for fifteen. And that was the only thing that I was out there at R.S. Chandler. And I know the fellas that handled that stuff. Now we'd be around a poker table playing poker, and the fellas would walk in there and send somebody out to, and get a dozen. I'd be on the table. I'd smoke them like that on the table. I'd never smoke one in my life. They used to tell me to light it. I'd take a match and hold it up this way. If it lights or if it didn't light, I'd never run my mouth for life. And they fellas say, well you bummed out that much drunk. Why you didn't? Well I didn't, I don't know. I never did pick up a bad habit. I never had a fight in my life. That's the truth. I didn't, I was a, I don't know, I just wanted to be a good fella. I never did like to do nothing bad. And if fellas were going to do something bad, he said, you stay in love with something bad. I'm with some bad boys. And they fellas say, well you bummed out that much drunk. Why you didn't? Well I didn't, I don't know, I never did pick up a bad habit. I never was a drunker. I never had a fight in my life. That's the truth. I didn't, I was a, I don't know, I just wanted to be a good fella. I never did like to do nothing bad. And if fellas were going to do something bad, he said, you stay in love with something bad. I was a bad boy. I never went to jail in my life. I wasn't going to be gambling. I went to jail many times in the region, the region, the giant book of gambling. Yeah. But outside of that, I never went to jail. Police never stopped me. I was sitting on the corner and the police walked up there hard, I'll never forget. And they wanted me to go, that's the during the time that they really segregated bars and so on. And they wanted me to go about three blocks and buy a beer. Well, the old man would have sold me the beer and I could have drank it in there. Not me, but the wrong person. But he got a father doing it. And went there and put the old man in jail. He said, no. He said, no. He says, so he asked, did they go run the place? I said, what did they say? The dagger told me, he's all right. He told him, he said, no, you're going to get that far. I do nothing like that. He said, not him. He ain't going to do that. He won't do that. He said, no, you're going to get that far. Because he put me in jail. Because he put me in jail. I told him what they put me in jail for. That's what he put me in jail for. I wasn't probably in no laws. And I was running the classic game, you see. I was running the poker game too. Because I didn't go down there and buy a beer in that white place. You going to put me in jail for that? So I told him, no, he said, he's all right. Don't worry about him. He's all right.

Well, did they take junk in those days? Did those fellas take junk in those days? Oh, yeah. They had junk back then. That's a terrible thing. I guess it was killing them off then like it was killing them all.

It wasn't as many. It wasn't as many them days as it is today. I lived over there 21 years at that corner house, with my wife. And I saw 95% of the dope addicts around here start off right on that corner. I know boys from a good family, swell boys. And I, you see, they had them big old doves. They'd keep them on the jaw like that. Of course, I'd have the light out. It'd be dark. And they're sitting on them. I step out of them sniff cocaine. I saw them shoot the needle right on that corner over there. See, on this side they had a big shed all the way around. And where the people lived upstairs, what they used to call them, Ferraros was their name. They lived upstairs. They had about three or four daughters and one son. Tony's one son, and they had three or four daughters. And when they'd close the place at night, those guys would get on those steps and shoot the needle. And you could see them, they'd take a beer top. And I don't know how they could do it and heat it. I guess it'd make it watery like when shoot the needle. That house there, Newhouse now, it was old how they? Right across the street? Yeah. Not that one next to it. Newhouse was pretty little old. I see many of them guys right up there. Kill them dead. Kill them dead. Overdose. I used to be out in the French quarters with the Sy brothers, Sam, Tony, and Russell, and all that side gang. Well, I used to be out there with those guys. And, uh... ... ... ... ... ... ...

segments.title: Opening, name spelling and reel change
segments.summary: Wilson spells his name; the interviewer notes this is reel 2, April 5, 1962.

segments.title: Young people freer now: ballroom age rules and halls
segments.summary: Wilson says people had a better time in the old days; 21 to enter ballrooms, chaperoned girls at Economy Hall, and his own gambling and not drinking.

segments.title: Lake resorts: Milneburg and West End
segments.summary: He recalls the lakefront resorts, camps with bands, and dancing for forty or fifty cents.

segments.title: Societies' yearly parades and the Jolly Boys picnic
segments.summary: Old benevolent societies paraded; the Jolly Boys still do, taking in members just for parade season and planning a picnic.

segments.title: Hiring bands for picnics and dances; Fred Minor's son and John Casimir
segments.summary: The club hires any good band; Fred Minor was a past president, his son played, and Wilson names John Casimir.

segments.title: Sam Morgan and Rena; musicians drinking and Punch Miller's illness
segments.summary: Sam Morgan played soft at Economy Hall while Rena played loud and drank; Punch Miller is recovering, and musicians bum all night.

segments.title: Who can join the club, and dues
segments.summary: Members are vouched for or investigated; dues are a dollar ten a month, with two meetings a month.

segments.title: Age limits, youngsters in the parade, pleasure fund and death fund
segments.summary: Members are 18 to 65; the Jolly Boys are for pleasure, with separate pleasure and death accounts.

segments.title: Death assessments and the Sons and Daughters societies
segments.summary: When a member dies each member pays a dollar; he explains other clubs and women's benevolent societies.

segments.title: Officers, meetings and the Wonder Boys club
segments.summary: Men can serve in women's clubs; meetings open with prayer; he dislikes the Wonder Boys for lack of benefits.

segments.title: Old-time parade clothes, umbrellas and the rough second line
segments.summary: Old parade dress was black suits; umbrellas and baskets cost a lot, and rough second liners trouble the parade.

segments.title: Election of officers and Wilson as vice president
segments.summary: Officers are elected in March and installed later; Wilson has been vice president about ten years.

segments.title: Showing the decorated fan and badge
segments.summary: Wilson shows his decorated fan and officer badge, who makes them, and the colors.

segments.title: Grand marshals, baskets and sashes
segments.summary: Grand marshals are tall men with large baskets and sashes; Willie Hicks and Cass are their marshals.

segments.title: Dispute over marshals at Sunday's parade; Slow Drag and Pork Chop
segments.summary: The club disliked marching behind the hired band's marshals; Wilson knows Slow Drag and Pork Chop, and a dancer named Rankin.

segments.title: Dancers and bystanders who turn up at funerals
segments.summary: They talk about a dancer who walks like an alligator and how crowds find a funeral.

segments.title: Papoose's funeral and the serenaders Walter, Sam and Noon
segments.summary: The son of Walter, a guitarist, died of an overdose; his funeral band stopped four hours at a joint.

segments.title: Rock and roll bands at the club's dances
segments.summary: The club has hired a young rock and roll band and Dookie Chase; the young people want rock and roll.

segments.title: Old-time brass bands and Carnival parades
segments.summary: He names Celestin, Louis and Joe Oliver as brass band players for parades; colored bands played all Carnival parades.

segments.title: Growing up in the Irish Channel; Army in 1917
segments.summary: He grew up in the Irish Channel, where one club paraded until 1917, then went into the Army.

segments.title: Uptown versus downtown entertainment and gambling
segments.summary: The Irish Channel had warehouses and gambling clubs; piano joints were downtown on Rampart Street.

segments.title: Piano players and bands meeting on trucks to advertise dances
segments.summary: He recalls pianists Burnell, Little Willie and Red Caillou, and bands on trucks meeting on corners.

segments.title: Gang Kid and the pianist Thomas
segments.summary: Wilson knows Gang Kid and recalls Thomas, a blues pianist at parties.

segments.title: Guitar players and serenaders: Rabbit, Walter, Noon and Sam
segments.summary: He knows Rabbit, Walter and Noon, who serenaded; serenading has dropped off and he has not seen Sam.

segments.title: Piano players in bars and the music box ending them
segments.summary: Pianists once played in every bar, but the jukebox took the work away.

segments.title: Respect then and now
segments.summary: Young people are freer now and show less respect; more wine is drunk today.

segments.title: Smoking hop, gambling and an arrest
segments.summary: Users once kept to themselves; Wilson never used drugs and was jailed for running a poker game after refusing to buy beer in a white bar.

segments.title: Dope addiction on the old corner
segments.summary: Addiction was less common then; he saw addicts start at his corner for 21 years.
